methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Problem and Solution
content: Problem: Students frequently overgeneralize the "-ed" rule for past tense, producing errors like "eated", "drinked", or "haved".

Solution: Group irregular verbs by semantic themes (Consumption & Possession) and teach them implicitly through a highly relatable context (a picnic adventure). Students internalize the correct irregular forms through repeated, meaningful exposure before explicit rule presentation.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Teacher pull-out rotation during independent time:
S1: vocabulary drill — teacher says Vietnamese/mime, student says English + makes sentence.
S2: grammar pattern practice — teacher asks "What did you eat/drink?" → student answers using key pattern.
S3: VC script rehearsal — student reads aloud, teacher gives pronunciation feedback.

methodology.title: 2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: Pull-out oral tasks (teacher does these with 1–2 students while class works):
S1 pull-out: Show flashcard of base verb (e.g., "eat") → student says past form ("ate"), meaning, and 1 sentence.
S2 pull-out: Give prompt ("You were hungry. What did you do?") → student answers using the key pattern.
S3 pull-out: Student reads S3 VC script aloud → teacher recasts irregular verb mispronunciations.

Communicative task (Step 5 — 10 min — MUST have real information gap): Students work in pairs. Each student has a card with half the details of a picnic. They ask questions to complete the menu and events. Materials needed: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B per pair (Section 8). Step-by-step:
Give Student A Card A and Student B Card B. Do not show cards.
Students take turns asking the provided questions to fill in their blanks.
Students produce: A complete list of what was eaten, drunk, and had at the picnic.
ate: Mime bringing food to the mouth and chewing.
drank: Mime holding a glass and tilting head back.
had: Hold both hands flat in front of the chest, gesturing ownership.
hungry/thirsty: Rub stomach (hungry) or touch throat (thirsty).
Common errors to watch during pull-out:
Error: "I eated the apple." → Recast: "Listen: I ate the apple. What did you eat?"
Error: "He drinked juice." → Recast: "He drank juice. What did he drink?"

listening_script.text: Yesterday, Max and Luna went to the park. They had a big picnic under a tree. First, they played games and ran on the grass. Soon, Max was very hungry. "Let's eat!" he said. He ate a big sandwich. The sandwich was delicious! Luna was thirsty after running. She drank cold apple juice. Then, they had some fresh fruit. They ate red apples and green grapes. "This is a great picnic," said Luna. They ate, drank, and had a wonderful time. Finally, they went home, feeling very full and happy.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Names one thing Max or Luna ate/drank at the picnic (e.g., "Max ate a sandwich").
Student B: Adds another food or drink using had (e.g., "Luna had some juice").
Goal: Use ate / drank / had correctly in past tense without prompting.

PULL-OUT TASK (S1):
— Show a picture of a picnic basket. Ask: "What did they have for lunch?"
— Scaffold weaker students: "Max ___ a ___. Luna ___ some ___."
— Target elicitation: ate / drank / had — confirm students DON'T say "eated" or "drinked".

COMMUNICATIVE TASK TIP:
— If students say 'eated' or 'drinked', model immediately: "We say ATE and DRANK — they are irregular!"
— Stronger students: chain 3 verbs: "First, they ATE... Then, they DRANK... Finally, they HAD..."

SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Tells one thing Max's family did on holiday (e.g., "They had a great time at the beach").
Student B: Continues with another detail (e.g., "Max ate ice cream and drank coconut juice").
Goal: Use ate / drank / had in a connected narrative — week 30 full mastery check.

PULL-OUT TASK (S3 — Communicative Task):
— Ask: "Can you describe Max's best holiday using all three verbs?"
— Target full retell: "First, they WENT to the beach. They ATE ice cream. They DRANK juice. They HAD a great time."
— Mastery check: student uses ate / drank / had fluently with sequence words.

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: "Tell me ONE thing Max ate and ONE thing he drank."
— Stronger students: invent their own holiday story using ate / drank / had / went.

STEM/CLIL Extension Notes (teacher only):

PART 6: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION (Station C — 15 min minimum)
Health: A Balanced Diet
[ALL] Read this: To stay healthy, we need a balanced diet. A balanced diet means eating different types of food. We need carbohydrates, like bread in a sandwich, to give us energy to run. We need vitamins from fresh fruit to keep us strong and prevent sickness. Finally, our body needs a lot of water to stay hydrated. A good picnic has all of these things!
The diagram shows: A Food Pyramid. At the bottom, bread and grains (carbohydrates). In the middle, colorful fruits and vegetables (vitamins). At the top, a glass of water (hydration).

teacher_contents.reading_passage: Max wrote a story about his best holiday. "Last year, we had a holiday at the beach. First, I swam in the ocean. I was tired and hungry! Then, my family had a big picnic on the sand. I ate a sandwich with cheese. It was delicious! My sister was thirsty, so she drank coconut juice. We had such a wonderful time. 'Best holiday ever!' I said."
teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• Full W30 mastery: ate / drank / had all appear naturally in the beach holiday story
• 'had' appears twice: had a holiday + had a wonderful time — both correct and natural
• Week 30 verb chain drill: 'We WENT to the beach (W29). We ATE, DRANK, and HAD a great time (W30).'
• Common student error chain: 'We haved... we eated... we drinked' — address all three at once
• Portfolio connection: students write their own 'best meal' story using ate / drank / had
